Question: What is your favorite science-related picture?
Answer: This is alien like looking creature is called as bacteriophage, it is a virus that infects and replicates within bacteria and archaea. 1. Attachment: The bacteriophage first attaches to specific receptors on the surface of the E. coli cell. 2. Penetration: Once attached, the bacteriophage injects its genetic material ( the one which looks like a thread) into the host bacteria. 3. Replication: Once inside the bacterial cell, the phage hijacks the host cell's machinery to replicate its genetic material and produce viral components. 4. Assembly: The newly synthesized viral components are then assembled into complete bacteriophage particles called as virions within the host cell 5. Lysis and Release: Once assembly is complete, the bacteriophage induces the host cell to undergo lysis, or cell rupture, releasing the newly formed virions into the surrounding environment. A bacteriophage infecting Escherichia coli (E. coli) 6. Infection of New Hosts: The released bacteriophages can then infect neighboring bacterial cells, continuing the infection cycle. This process of infection, replication, and lysis can lead to the rapid spread of bacteriophages within bacteria.

Question: Is buying flat a scam, considered that you are buying one more stack above another and you do not own the land?
Answer: No you actually own a part of the plot. There is something called UDS ( Undivided Share ). It's the portion of the land held by the buyer of the flat in an apartment or a plot on which the whole structure is built. The area of UDS also depends upon how much percentage of area you own in the flat. Although you get a share , the shared land would not have any specific boundaries. But incase if the apartment you buy is demolished or reconstructed or it has been acquired by the government, you get the compensation depending on the percentage of undivided land share (UDS) you own in that plot. The simple formula to calculate UDS is (The Individual apartment built-up area/ Sum of all apartment’s built up area) * Total land area

Longyearbyen, Norway This remote, arctic town located in the Svalbard Islands has a unique law that forbids dying. The reason behind this prohibition is environmental: the permafrost in the area preserves bodies so well that they don’t decompose properly. Back in 1917, a deadly strain of flu hit this town and many residents were dead and their bodies were buried in the ground .13 years later when someone happened to dig the bodies, they were horrified to realize that these bodies were not decomposing as the ground was so cold that their bodies were completely preserved along with those deadly strains of flu, and lives samples of spanish flu were extracted from the dead bodies. Realizing the potential dangers, the leaders of this town enacted a law where dying is not allowed in their town. To enact this rule, they tried to keep their population young In case you were wondering how people die nowadays, well, anyone nearing death is often taken to the mainland and other parts of Norway where this law seize to exist Itsukushima, Japan Itsukushima is an island in Japan. In the 8th century, a sanctuary dedicated to the three Shinto divinities was built on this coast, making this a sacred place. To preserve the purity of the sanctuary, it is forbidden to bury the dead or give birth in this island. Answer: Imagine getting a MILLION DOLLARS for just spilling coffee on your lap McDonald’s has been involved in numerous lawsuits over the years, but one of the most publicized and often referred to as the most funniest and rediculous is the hot coffee lawsuit from 1990s In 1992, Stella Liebeck purchased a cup of hot coffee which costed around 49 cents from a McDonald’s drive-through and suffered third-degree burns after the coffee spilled in her lap. Liebeck's attorneys argued that, at 180–190 °F (82–88 °C), McDonald's coffee was defective, and more likely to cause serious injury than coffee served at any other establishment. The jury found that McDonald's was the one responsible for the incident and awarded Liebeck a net $160,000 to cover medical expenses, and $2.7 million (equivalent to $5,300,000 in 2022) the equivalent of two days of McDonald's coffee sales. The trial judge later reduced the punitive damages to three times the amount of the compensatory damages, totalling $640,000.
